2.text: credence to such complaints. The tales show plainly enough that in the old

3.text: war times the sensuality of this people was just as strong as it is at present.

4.text: Still, many of the Chukchee girls are chaste until their marriage; and, in

5.text: comparison with the other tribes of this country, the Chukchee are considerably

6.text: more decent. Among the Russian and Russianized natives throughout the

7.text: whole northeast, from the Lena River to Kamchatka, hardly any girl remains

8.text: virgin until her marriage. Most of them begin sexual life with the first traces

9.text: of maturity, being but fifteen or sixteen, and sometimes only twelve or thirteen

10.text: years old, and quite immature. All kinds of cases of adultery and incest also

11.text: occur, even in the families of the clergy, and are participated in by monks

12.text: and missionaries. Of this I shall speak later on in more detail. Among the

13.text: Russian creoles even new proverbs were created, which have reference to this

14.text: sexual promiscuity: for instance, “Married is not sold for slavery” (вѣнчалась,

15.text: не продалась); “A woman is not a muffin, you cannot eat her up all alone”

16.text: (баба не калачъ, одинъ не съѣшь); “A finger in a ring is not a bolt on the

17.text: door” (палецъ въ кольцѣ, не замокъ на крыльцѣ); “Whatsoever bull may have

18.text: leaped, the calf is our own” (чей бы быкъ ни скакалъ, а теленочекъ нашъ).

19.text: The Reindeer Chukchee girls grow mature later than those of the neigh-

20.text: boring tribes;¹ and since the Chukchee camps are thinly scattered over the

21.text: tundra, many of their girls have no chance to meet friendly young men.

22.text: Being shy and proud by nature, a Reindeer Chukchee girl would avoid flirting

23.text: with a man wholly unknown to her. She would prefer to become intimately

24.text: acquainted with him, and then perhaps have him for a husband.

25.text: Still, not a few of the girls have lovers and bear children without being

26.text: married. The language has a special term for illegitimate, illegal love, viˊn˙-

27.text: vɪtkurkɪn (“Thou keepest up a clandestine love”), derived from the adverb

28.text: viˊn˙vᴇ (“clandestinely”). Natural children are kept on the same footing as

29.text: others; the more so, as frequent divorces often leave the woman with her

30.text: children in the family of her father, and it is rather difficult to distinguish

31.text: between these latter and the natural children. The Chukchee say, “When a

32.text: child is born, we rejoice over it, no matter whether it is natural or legitimate.”

33.text: I once met a family on the Dry Anui River, consisting of an old father, a

34.text: daughter not very young, and four grown-up sons. The daughter was con-

35.text: siderably older than her brothers, and since their mother had been dead quite

36.text: a long time, she had taken care of the house for the previous fifteen years.

37.text: Moreover, when she was quite young, her father had made her the “principal

38.text: heir” to the herd.² Now, two of the brothers were already married, and each

39.text: of them had a child. The girl had borne a son some five years before. This

40.text: son was proclaimed the principal heir; and now it was presumed that he would
